findings.title: Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure
findings.body: FixedQueuePool creates each worker queue with queue.Queue() and submit() always put()s without a max size. The strategy docstring claims natural backpressure when queues fill, but an unbounded queue never blocks the Arroyo poll thread. If result handling is slower than ingest, every message is copied into process memory and the consumer keeps fetching. A slow subscription or DB stall can grow memory until the process is OOM-killed, and offsets still outstanding will be reprocessed after restart.

findings.title: Kafka commits are issued from a background thread
findings.body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy starts a daemon commit thread that calls the Arroyo commit callback about once a second. That callback is only safe on the strategy thread (poll/join); it mutates consumer offset state that the processor also touches. Committing from another thread can race with poll, rebalance, and shutdown, producing incorrect commits, exceptions in the consumer, or a commit that does not match what the processor believes is safe.

findings.title: Strategy close kills the factory-owned worker pool
findings.body: The queue pool and its threads are created once on ResultsStrategyFactory, but SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() and terminate() call queue_pool.shutdown(), which sets worker.shutdown, calls Queue.shutdown(), and joins the workers. Arroyo closes the strategy on every partition revoke/rebalance and then calls create_with_partitions again on the same factory. The next strategy still holds the already-shut-down pool, so later submit() calls fail or drop work and the consumer cannot process after the first rebalance or restart of the assignment.

findings.title: Submit failures are acknowledged and never retried
findings.body: If decode, grouping, or queue put raises, submit() logs and immediately add_offset/complete_offset for that broker offset. The commit loop then treats the message as fully processed and commits past it. Unlike RunTask, this does not crash the consumer, retry, or DLQ. A transient error (DB blip during grouping, queue already shut down, codec glitch that escapes decode_payload) permanently skips the uptime result, so incidents derived from that check are never created.

findings.title: Shutdown abandons queued work and can skip the final commit
findings.body: close() stops the commit thread before pool.shutdown(). shutdown() sets worker.shutdown = True and then shuts the queues down. A worker blocked in get() may process one item and then exit because the flag is set, leaving the rest of the queue unprocessed. Those offsets stay outstanding, and because the commit thread has already been joined they are never committed. join() also ignores the timeout argument and close() joins each worker for up to 5s sequentially, so a 20-worker pool can block shutdown for over a minute and still drop the tail. After every deploy or rebalance those messages are redelivered, and any handler that is not idempotent can double-write.

findings.title: Queue-depth test races the workers
findings.body: test_stats_reporting submits 10 items and immediately asserts get_stats()["total_items"] > 0. Workers are already running and the processor is a no-op, so the queues can be empty before that assertion. The test will flake under load even though the pool is behaving correctly. The same pattern does not wait until in-flight work finishes: qsize() is 0 as soon as a worker has dequeued an item, so wait_until_empty can return while processing is still running.

findings.title: Error-handling test asserts the opposite of the implementation
findings.body: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling says processing errors must not block commits, but it asserts that no offset was committed after a handler exception. OrderedQueueWorker catches that exception and complete_offset() still runs, so the commit thread will commit the partition within about a second. The test only sleeps ~0.2s after the queue drains, so it passes only when the commit loop has not fired yet and fails when it has. It neither locks the intended behavior nor is stable.
